# Introduction

# Question a

Each of the $n$ birds is caught exactly once. The capture day of bird $i$ is denoted by $t_i$ and is treated as fixed. Every bird moults at the same constant rate, with moult lasting $\tau$ days for all birds. The start of moult for bird $i$, $T_i$, is an unobserved random variable, where

$$
T_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad f_T(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \text{exp}\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(x-\mu)^2\right), \qquad i = 1, \dots, n.
$$ {#eq-startdate}

Let $Z = \frac{T_i -\mu}{\sigma} \sim \text{N}(0,1)$ and let $\Phi$ denote the corresponding CDF. In the Type 1 model, only the status ($s_i \in \{1,2,3\}$) of each bird is observed.

For $s_i=3$, bird $i$ has not yet started moult:

$$
P(t_i) = \text{Pr}(T_i > t_i) = \text{Pr}\left(Z > \frac{t_i -\mu}{\sigma}\right) = 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{t_i - \mu}{\sigma}\right). 
$$ {#eq-P}

For $s_i=2$, bird $i$ is currently moulting:

$$
Q(t_i) = \text{Pr}(t_i - \tau \leq T_i \leq t_i) = \text{Pr}\left(\frac{t_i-\tau-\mu}{\sigma} \leq Z \leq \frac{t_i-\mu}{\sigma}\right) = \Phi\left(\frac{t_i-\mu}{\sigma}\right) - \Phi\left(\frac{t_i -\tau - \mu}{\sigma}\right).
$$ {#eq-Q}

For $s_i=1$, bird $i$ has finished moulting:

$$
R(t_i) = \text{Pr}(T_i \leq t_i - \tau) = \text{Pr}\left(Z \leq \frac{t_i -\tau- \mu}{\sigma}\right) = \Phi\left(\frac{t_i-\tau-\mu}{\sigma}\right).
$$ {#eq-R}

Given $t_i$, the status $s_i$ is a single categorical draw with probabilities $P(t_i), Q(t_i)$ and $R(t_i)$, given in @eq-P, @eq-Q and @eq-R. Thus, the conditional probability of $s_i$ can be written as

$$
\text{Pr}(s_i \mid t_i,\mu,\sigma^2,\tau) = P(t_i)^{\text{I}\{s_i=3\}} \, Q(t_i)^{\text{I}\{s_i=2\}} \, R(t_i)^{\text{I}\{s_i=1\}}.
$$ {#eq-status}

Since the birds are independent, the likelihood is the product of @eq-status over all $n$ birds

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(\boldsymbol{s}, \boldsymbol{t}, \mu, \sigma^2, \tau) & = \prod^n_{i=1} P(t_i)^{\text{I}\{s_i=3\}} \, Q(t_i)^{\text{I}\{s_i=2\}} \, R(t_i)^{\text{I}\{s_i=1\}} \\
& = \prod^{n}_{i=1} \left[1 - \Phi(\frac{t_i-\mu}{\sigma})\right]^{\text{I}\{s_i=3\}} \, \left[\Phi(\frac{t_i-\mu}{\sigma}) - \Phi(\frac{t_i -\tau - \mu}{\sigma})\right]^{\text{I}\{s_i=2\}} \, \left[\Phi(\frac{t_i-\tau-\mu}{\sigma})\right]^{\text{I}\{s_i=1\}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-lik1}

On any capture day $t$, the population consists of birds which belong to three different states. Birds have either not yet started to moult, are undergoing moult or have completed moult. These states occur in proportions $P(t), Q(t)$ and $R(t)$, which depend on $t$ through $\mu$, $\sigma^2$ and $\tau$. Thus, the moult index has a mixture distribution with a point mass at 0 and 1 with weights $P(t)$ and $R(t)$, respectively, as well as a continuous component on ($0,1$) with weight $Q(t)$. In the Type 1 model, the moult index is not observed. We only observe the state that bird $i$ belongs to. Thus, each bird contributes the weight of the state it belongs to $P(t_i)$, $Q(t_i)$ or $R(t_i)$, to @eq-lik1.

# Question b

In the Type 2 model, the moult scores ($y_i$) for birds that are currently moulting are observed. The birds are grouped according to their states. Let $\mathcal{F} = \{i : s_i = 1\}$ denote the set of birds that have already moulted, $\mathcal{M} = \{i : s_i = 2\}$ denote the set of birds that are undergoing moult and $\mathcal{N} = \{i : s_i = 3\}$ denote the set of birds that have not yet started to moult. Let $m = |\mathcal{M}|$ be the number of birds currently moulting.

For a bird undergoing moult, the linear assumption gives $T_i = t_i - y_i\tau$. The probability density function of its observed moult score is

$$
f_y(y_i) = \tau f_T(t_i - y_i\tau) \qquad 0<y_i<1.
$$ {#eq-fy}

The likelihood contributions of birds that have already moulted and birds that have not yet started to moult are the same as in the Type 1 model. Thus, the Type 2 likelihood is

$$
L(\boldsymbol{s}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{t}, \mu, \sigma^2, \tau) = \prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} R(t_i) \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \tau f_T(t_i - y_i\tau) \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{N}} P(t_i),
$$ {#eq-lik2}

and the joint posterior distribution is

$$
\pi(\mu, \sigma^2, \tau \mid \boldsymbol{s}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{t}) \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} R(t_i) \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \tau f_T(t_i - y_i\tau) \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{N}} P(t_i) \, \pi(\mu) \, \pi(\sigma^2) \, \pi(\tau),
$$ {#eq-post2}

with the following prior distributions 

$$
\mu \sim \text{Uniform}(100,160), \quad \sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(1,1), \quad \tau \sim \text{Uniform}(50,180).
$$ {#eq-priors}

## Data augmentation

The probabilities $R(t_i)$ and $P(t_i)$ in @eq-post2 are integrals over the unobserved start date

$$
\begin{aligned}
R(t_i) & = \text{Pr}(T_i \leq t_i - \tau) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_T(T_i)\, \text{I}\{T_i \leq t_i - \tau\}\, dT_i, \\
P(t_i) & = \text{Pr}(T_i > t_i) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_T(T_i)\, \text{I}\{T_i > t_i\}\, dT_i.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-RPintegrals}

The status is fully determined by the start date ($T_i$), so each integrand in @eq-RPintegrals is the joint density of the start date and the bird's status

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(T_i, s_i = 1 \mid \mu, \sigma^2, \tau) &= f_T(T_i)\, \text{I}\{T_i \leq t_i - \tau\}, \\
p(T_i, s_i = 3 \mid \mu, \sigma^2) &= f_T(T_i)\, \text{I}\{T_i > t_i\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-jointTs}

$T_i$ for $i \in \mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{N}$ is treated as a latent variable and samples are drawn from the augmented posterior

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\boldsymbol{T}_{(\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{N})}, \mu, \sigma^2, \tau \mid \boldsymbol{s}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{t}) & \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} \left[f_T(T_i)\, \text{I}\{T_i \leq t_i - \tau\}\right] \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \left[\tau f_T(t_i - y_i\tau)\right] \\
& \times \prod_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \left[f_T(T_i)\, \text{I}\{T_i > t_i\}\right] \, \pi(\mu) \, \pi(\sigma^2) \, \pi(\tau).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-augpost}

Integrating out each $T_i$ in @eq-augpost returns $R(t_i)$ or $P(t_i)$, so that

$$
\int \pi(\boldsymbol{T}_{(\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{N})}, \mu, \sigma^2, \tau \mid \boldsymbol{s}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{t})\, d\boldsymbol{T}_{(\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{N})} = \pi(\mu, \sigma^2, \tau \mid \boldsymbol{s}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{t}).
$$ {#eq-marginal}

The posterior distribution of interest, @eq-post2, is the marginal distribution of the augmented posterior. Thus, the draws of $(\mu, \sigma^2, \tau)$ from a sampler targeting the augmented posterior are draws from the required posterior. No latent variables are needed for the moulting birds, since $T_i = t_i - y_i\tau$ is a deterministic function of $\tau$ for $i \in \mathcal{M}$. Since $0<y_i<1$, the condition $t_i -\tau \leq T_i \leq t_i$ is always satisfied.

### Conditional distributions of $T_i$

The conditional distributions of the latent start dates are the same truncated normal distributions as in the Type 1 Gibbs sampler:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_i \mid \cdot &\sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\, \text{I}\{T_i \leq t_i - \tau\}, & i \in \mathcal{F}, \\
T_i \mid \cdot &\sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\, \text{I}\{T_i > t_i\}, & i \in \mathcal{N}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-condT}

### Conditional distribution of $\mu$

From @eq-augpost, the full conditional distribution of $\mu$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\mu \mid \cdot) & \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} \left[f_T(T_i)\right] \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \left[f_T(t_i - y_i\tau)\right] \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \left[f_T(T_i)\right] \, \pi(\mu) \\
& \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} \left[f_T(T_i)\right] \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \left[f_T(T_i)\right] \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \left[f_T(T_i)\right] \, \pi(\mu) \\
& \propto \prod_{i=1}^n f_T(T_i)\, \pi(\mu) \\
& = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma} \exp\left(-\frac{(T_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \text{I}\{100 \leq \mu \leq 160\} \\
&\propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (T_i - \mu)^2\right) \text{I}\{100 \leq \mu \leq 160\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $\bar{T} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n T_i$. Expanding the sum of squares gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n (T_i - \mu)^2 &= \sum_{i=1}^n \big[(T_i - \bar{T}) + (\bar{T} - \mu)\big]^2 \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n (T_i - \bar{T})^2 + 2(\bar{T} - \mu)\sum_{i=1}^n (T_i - \bar{T}) + n(\bar{T} - \mu)^2 \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n (T_i - \bar{T})^2 + n(\bar{T} - \mu)^2,
\end{aligned}
$$

since $\sum_{i=1}^n (T_i - \bar{T}) = 0$. Thus,

$$
\pi(\mu \mid \cdot) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\mu - \bar{T})^2\right) \text{I}\{100 \leq \mu \leq 160\}.
$$

This is the kernel of a truncated normal distribution

$$
\mu \mid \cdot \sim \text{N}\left(\bar{T}, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) \text{I}\{100 \leq \mu \leq 160\}.
$$ {#eq-condmu}

For the moulting birds, $T_i = t_i - y_i\tau$ is used in $\bar{T}$.

### Conditional distribution of $\sigma^2$

Let $S = \sum_{i=1}^n (T_i - \mu)^2$. From @eq-augpost, the full conditional distribution of $\sigma^2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\sigma^2 \mid \cdot) & \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} \left[f_T(T_i)\right] \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \left[f_T(t_i - y_i\tau)\right] \prod_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \left[f_T(T_i)\right] \, \pi(\sigma^2) \\
& \propto \prod_{i=1}^n f_T(T_i)\, \pi(\sigma^2) \\
& \propto (\sigma^2)^{-n/2} \exp\left(-\frac{S}{2\sigma^2}\right) (\sigma^2)^{-2} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\right) \\
& = (\sigma^2)^{-\left(\frac{n}{2} + 1\right) - 1} \exp\left(-\frac{1 + \frac{S}{2}}{\sigma^2}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the kernel of an inverse-gamma distribution

$$
\sigma^2 \mid \cdot \sim \text{IG}\left(\frac{n}{2} + 1,\; 1 + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n (T_i - \mu)^2\right).
$$ {#eq-condsigma2}

@eq-condsigma2 differs from the Type 1 conditional given in the assignment, which corresponds to the prior $\pi(\sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2$ as opposed to $\text{IG}(1, 1)$.

### Conditional distribution of $\tau$

From @eq-augpost, with $T_i=t_i-y_i\tau$ for the moulting birds, the full conditional distribution of $\tau$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi(\tau \mid \cdot) & \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} \left[\text{I}\{T_i \leq t_i - \tau\}\right] \, \prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \left[\tau f_T(t_i - y_i\tau)\right] \, \pi(\tau) \\
& \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \tau f_T(t_i - y_i\tau) \prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} \text{I}\{T_i \leq t_i - \tau\}\, \text{I}\{50 \leq \tau \leq 180\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The moulting birds contribute

$$
\prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \tau f_T(t_i - y_i\tau) \propto \tau^m \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} (t_i - \mu - y_i\tau)^2\right).
$$

Expanding the square gives

$$
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} (t_i - \mu - y_i\tau)^2 = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} (t_i - \mu)^2 - 2\tau \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} y_i (t_i - \mu) + \tau^2 \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} y_i^2,
$$

where the first term does not depend on $\tau$. Thus, 

$$
\prod_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \tau f_T(t_i - y_i\tau) \propto \tau^m \exp\left(-\beta\tau^2 + \gamma\tau\right),
$$

where $\beta = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} y_i^2}{2\sigma^2}$ and $\gamma = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} y_i (t_i - \mu)}{\sigma^2}.$

The finished birds only contribute through their indicators. The product equals one only if the condition holds for every finished bird, so

$$
\prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}} \text{I}\{T_i \leq t_i - \tau\} = \text{I}\{\tau \leq \underset{i \in \mathcal{F}}{\text{min}}(t_i - T_i)\}
$$

Let $h = \underset{i \in \mathcal{F}}{\text{min}}(t_i - T_i)$. Thus, the duration of moult cannot exceed the time between the start date and the capture date of any finished bird.

Combining these two terms with the prior gives

$$
\pi(\tau \mid \cdot) \propto \tau^{m} \exp\left(-\beta\tau^2 + \gamma\tau\right) \text{I}\{50 \leq \tau \leq \min(180, h)\}.
$$

This is the kernel of a Modified-Half-Normal distribution (Sun et al., 2021)

$$
\tau \mid \cdot \sim \text{MHN}\left(m + 1,\; \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} y_i^2}{2\sigma^2},\; \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} y_i (t_i - \mu)}{\sigma^2}\right) \text{I}\{50 \leq \tau \leq \min(180, h)\}.
$$ {#eq-condtau}

In the Type 1 model, $\tau$ appears only in the indicators and has a uniform conditional distribution. In the Type 2 model, the observed moult scores result in a non-uniformly shaped conditional of $\tau$. Sampling from @eq-condtau can be simplified using a further data augmentation step (Lemma 5 of Sun et al., 2021). The form of this data augmentation depends on the sign of $\gamma$. Since $y_i > 0$, $\gamma \geq 0$ if and only if $\mu \leq \bar{t}_y = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} y_i t_i \big/ \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} y_i$.

When $\gamma \geq 0$, a latent variable $V$ is introduced such that $V \mid \tau \sim \text{Poisson}(\gamma\tau)$. Multiplying the conditional distribution of $\tau$ by the Poisson probability gives

$$
\tau^{m} e^{-\beta\tau^2 + \gamma\tau} \cdot \frac{e^{-\gamma\tau}(\gamma\tau)^V}{V!} \propto \tau^{m + V} e^{-\beta\tau^2},
$$

so the term $e^{\gamma\tau}$ cancels. Substituting $W = \tau^2$ and noting that the indicator only involves $\tau$,

$$
W \mid V \sim \text{Gamma}\left(\frac{m + 1 + V}{2},\; \beta\right) \text{I}\{50^2 \leq W \leq \min(180, h)^2\},
$$ {#eq-augV}

where $\beta$ is the rate parameter. When $\gamma = 0$, $V = 0$ and @eq-augV reduces to a truncated $\text{Gamma}\left(\frac{m+1}{2}, \beta\right)$ distribution.

When $\gamma < 0$, a latent variable $U$ is introduced instead. Using the parameterisation $\text{GIG}(p, a, b)$ with density proportional to $u^{p-1}\exp\{-(au + b/u)/2\}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
U \mid \tau &\sim \text{GIG}\left(\frac{1}{2},\; 1,\; \gamma^2\tau^2\right), \\
W \mid U &\sim \text{Gamma}\left(\frac{m + 1}{2},\; \beta + \frac{\gamma^2}{2U}\right) \text{I}\{50^2 \leq W \leq \min(180, h)^2\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-augU}

Under this parameterisation of the GIG distribution the rate parameter is $\beta + \frac{\gamma^2}{2U}$. Sun et al. (2021) state the rate as $\beta + \frac{\gamma^2}{U}$, which corresponds to a different parameterisation of the GIG distribution.

In both cases, the truncated gamma distribution can be sampled exactly using the inverse CDF method, after which $\tau = \sqrt{W}$. The latent variable $V$ or $U$ is redrawn given the current $\tau$ at every iteration and then discarded, so the conditionals of the other parameters are unchanged.

### The Gibbs sampling algorithm

1.  Initialise $\mu^{(0)} \sim \text{U}(100, 160)$, $\sigma^{2(0)} \sim \text{IG}(1, 1)$ and $\tau^{(0)} \sim \text{U}(50, 180)$. Draw $T_i^{(0)}$ for $i \in \mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{N}$ from their truncated normal conditional distributions, @eq-condT, given these values.
2.  For $k = 1, \dots, K$:
    a.  For $i \in \mathcal{F}$, draw $T_i^{(k)} \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mu^{(k-1)}, \sigma^{2(k-1)}\big)\, \text{I}\{T_i \leq t_i - \tau^{(k-1)}\}$.
    b.  For $i \in \mathcal{N}$, draw $T_i^{(k)} \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mu^{(k-1)}, \sigma^{2(k-1)}\big)\, \text{I}\{T_i > t_i\}$.
    c.  For $i \in \mathcal{M}$, set $T_i^{(k)} = t_i - y_i \tau^{(k-1)}$.
    d.  Draw $\mu^{(k)} \sim \text{N}\big(\bar{T}^{(k)}, \sigma^{2(k-1)}/n\big)\, \text{I}\{100 \leq \mu \leq 160\}$.
    e.  Draw $\sigma^{2(k)} \sim \text{IG}\big(\frac{n}{2} + 1,\; 1 + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n (T_i^{(k)} - \mu^{(k)})^2\big)$.
    f.  Compute $h^{(k)} = \min_{i \in \mathcal{F}} (t_i - T_i^{(k)})$, and $\beta^{(k)}$ and $\gamma^{(k)}$ evaluated at $\mu^{(k)}$ and $\sigma^{2(k)}$. If $\gamma^{(k)} \geq 0$, draw $V \sim \text{Poisson}\big(\gamma^{(k)}\tau^{(k-1)}\big)$ and $W \sim \text{Gamma}\big(\frac{m+1+V}{2}, \beta^{(k)}\big)$; otherwise, draw $U \sim \text{GIG}\big(\frac{1}{2}, 1, (\gamma^{(k)}\tau^{(k-1)})^2\big)$ and $W \sim \text{Gamma}\big(\frac{m+1}{2}, \beta^{(k)} + \frac{(\gamma^{(k)})^2}{2U}\big)$. In both cases, $W$ is truncated to $[50^2, \min(180, h^{(k)})^2]$. Set $\tau^{(k)} = \sqrt{W}$.
3.  After discarding a burn-in period, retain the draws $(\mu^{(k)}, \sigma^{2(k)}, \tau^{(k)})$ as samples from the posterior $\pi(\mu, \sigma^2, \tau \mid \boldsymbol{s}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{t})$. The latent variables $T_i^{(k)}$, $V$ and $U$ are discarded.

## Question c

We sample from the likelihood surface using a Metropolis Hastings algorithm. However we have the problem that the steps of our random walk are drawn a multivariate normal distribution. But each of our three parameters do not have support over the entire real line: $\mu$, which determines the average start time, is constrained by a uniform prior to be situated between 100--160; $\tau$, which determines the speed of moulting, is also contrainted by its prior to be situated within 50--180; finally the variance is strictly positive. We define the following transformations:\
$$\begin{aligned}
f(\mu)&=\text{logit} \frac{\mu-100}{60}\\
g(\tau)&=\text{logit} \frac{\tau-50}{130}\\
h(\sigma^2)&= \log \sigma^2
\end{aligned}$$ These transformation each have support over the entire real line; thus we may perform our random walk over this transformed space. Since we are unsure how our parameters are correlated; to begin with, the steps of our random walk are drawn from:\
$$e_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,c \,I)$$ For some constant $c$. However, when back transform (let $\theta$ be our original parameters and $\phi$ their transformations) we must include the jacobian term in the posterior likelihood in order to ensure that the Metropolis-Hasting algorithm converges to the appropriate likelihood; the log-likelihood becomes: $$L(\theta)+\log(\pi(\theta))+\log|J(\phi)|$$ Where $J(\phi)$ is the Jacobian of our transformation. However, we would like to tune our random walk to have a more appropriate covaraince matrix; to achieve this we utilize 3000 burnin iterations and estimate the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ of our transformed parameters on these iterations. Them each of our retained draws each have their random walk drawn from: $$e\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$$ And the Metropolis Hastings algorithm algorithm proceeds as per usual. We obtain the following estimates of our parameters and as well as 95% credible intervals on them:

| Parameter                  | Posterior mean | 2.5% quantile | 97.5% quantile |
|:---------------------------|---------------:|--------------:|---------------:|
| Mean start time ($\mu$)    |         130.67 |        114.61 |         152.40 |
| Variance ($\sigma\^2$)     |         317.18 |        195.19 |         525.00 |
| Moulting duration ($\tau$) |          92.79 |         56.43 |         128.40 |

: Posterior mean estimates and 95% credible intervals for the Type 3 moulting model. {#tbl-mh-estimates}

# Question c

```{r}
#| label: setup-c
#| echo: false

# Load required libraries:
library(coda)      # MCMC diagnostics
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

# Load data (path is relative to this .qmd file):
dat = read.csv("sanderlings.csv")

# Classification scheme from the assignment:
# 3 = not yet started, 1 = finished, 2 = currently moulting
dat$status = ifelse(dat$MIndex == 0, 3,
             ifelse(dat$MIndex == 1, 1, 2))

# The Type 3 model uses only the moulting birds:
moulting = subset(dat, status == 2)
day = moulting$Day        # capture day t_i
y   = moulting$MIndex     # moult index y_i, 0 < y_i < 1
m   = length(day)         # number of moulting birds
```

```{r}
#| label: mh-functions
#| echo: false

# Log posterior on the original scale, theta = (mu, sigma2, tau):
log_post = function(theta) {
  mu = theta[1]; sigma2 = theta[2]; tau = theta[3]

  # Outside the prior support the posterior is 0 (log posterior = -Inf):
  if (mu <= 100 || mu >= 160 || tau <= 50 || tau >= 180 || sigma2 <= 0) return(-Inf)
  sigma = sqrt(sigma2)

  # log Q(t_i) = log[Phi(a_i) - Phi(b_i)], computed on the log scale:
  log_a = pnorm((day - mu) / sigma,       log.p = TRUE)
  log_b = pnorm((day - tau - mu) / sigma, log.p = TRUE)
  log_Q = log_a + log1p(-exp(log_b - log_a))

  # Type 3 log-likelihood:
  log_lik = sum(log(tau) + dnorm(day - y * tau, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE) - log_Q)

  # Log prior (uniform priors are constant, IG(1,1) for sigma2):
  log_prior = -2 * log(sigma2) - 1 / sigma2

  log_lik + log_prior
}

# Transformations to the unconstrained scale phi:
logit = function(p) log(p / (1 - p))
expit = function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

to_phi = function(theta) c(logit((theta[1] - 100) / 60),
                           log(theta[2]),
                           logit((theta[3] - 50) / 130))

to_theta = function(phi) c(100 + 60 * expit(phi[1]),
                           exp(phi[2]),
                           50 + 130 * expit(phi[3]))

# Log target on the phi scale = log posterior + log|Jacobian|:
log_target = function(phi) {
  p1 = expit(phi[1]); p3 = expit(phi[3])
  log_jac = log(60 * p1 * (1 - p1)) + phi[2] + log(130 * p3 * (1 - p3))
  val = log_post(to_theta(phi)) + log_jac
  if (!is.finite(val)) val = -Inf
  val
}

# Random walk Metropolis-Hastings, proposal phi* = phi + e, e ~ N(0, Sigma):
run_mh = function(phi_start, Sigma, n_iter) {
  L = t(chol(Sigma))
  theta_draws = matrix(NA, n_iter, 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("mu", "sigma2", "tau")))
  phi_draws   = matrix(NA, n_iter, 3)
  phi = phi_start
  lp  = log_target(phi)
  n_accept = 0

  for (k in 1:n_iter) {
    phi_prop = phi + as.vector(L %*% rnorm(3))   # propose
    lp_prop  = log_target(phi_prop)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_prop - lp) {          # accept with prob min(1, r)
      phi = phi_prop; lp = lp_prop; n_accept = n_accept + 1
    }
    phi_draws[k, ]   = phi
    theta_draws[k, ] = to_theta(phi)
  }
  list(theta = theta_draws, phi = phi_draws, accept_rate = n_accept / n_iter)
}

# Random starting values: mu and tau uniform over their prior ranges,
# sigma2 log-uniform on (10, 2000):
random_start = function() {
  repeat {
    theta0 = c(runif(1, 100, 160), exp(runif(1, log(10), log(2000))), runif(1, 50, 180))
    if (is.finite(log_post(theta0))) return(theta0)
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: mh-run
#| echo: false
#| cache: true

# Set seed for reproducibility:
set.seed(2026)

# Pilot run 1: independent proposals, Sigma = 0.05 I
pilot1 = run_mh(to_phi(random_start()), diag(0.05, 3), 5000)

# Pilot run 2: covariance of the second half of pilot 1, scaled by 2.38^2/d
d = 3
Sigma1 = (2.38^2 / d) * cov(pilot1$phi[2501:5000, ]) + diag(1e-8, 3)
pilot2 = run_mh(pilot1$phi[5000, ], Sigma1, 10000)

# Final (fixed) proposal covariance from pilot 2:
Sigma_tuned = (2.38^2 / d) * cov(pilot2$phi) + diag(1e-8, 3)

# Main run: 3 chains x 50 000 iterations from random starting values:
n_iter   = 50000
n_chains = 3
starts   = lapply(1:n_chains, function(j) random_start())
mh_runs  = lapply(starts, function(th0) run_mh(to_phi(th0), Sigma_tuned, n_iter))
```

```{r}
#| label: mh-diagnostics
#| echo: false

# Add sigma = sqrt(sigma2) and store as coda objects:
mh_all = mcmc.list(lapply(mh_runs, function(r)
  mcmc(cbind(r$theta, sigma = sqrt(r$theta[, "sigma2"])))))

# Burn-in:
burn    = 5000
mh_post = window(mh_all, start = burn + 1)

# Convergence diagnostics on the retained draws:
rhat = gelman.diag(mh_post, multivariate = FALSE)$psrf[, "Point est."]
ess  = effectiveSize(mh_post)

# All chains stacked:
mh_mat = as.matrix(mh_post)

# Posterior summaries:
post_summary = function(M) {
  t(apply(M, 2, function(x) c(mean   = mean(x),
                              sd     = sd(x),
                              q2.5   = unname(quantile(x, 0.025)),
                              median = median(x),
                              q97.5  = unname(quantile(x, 0.975)))))
}
mh_summary = post_summary(mh_mat)

# Values used in the text:
acc_rates = sapply(mh_runs, function(r) r$accept_rate)
cor_mat   = cor(mh_mat[, c("mu", "sigma2", "tau")])
```

# Question d

```{r}
#| label: stan-model
#| echo: false

# Type 3 model written in Stan:
modelString = "
  data {
    int<lower=1> m;                    // number of moulting birds
    vector[m] t;                       // capture day of each bird
    vector<lower=0, upper=1>[m] y;     // moult index
  }

  parameters {
    real<lower=100, upper=160> mu;     // mean start date of moult
    real<lower=0> sigma2;              // variance of start dates
    real<lower=50, upper=180> tau;     // duration of moult
  }

  transformed parameters {
    real<lower=0> sigma = sqrt(sigma2);
  }

  model {
    // Priors:
    mu     ~ uniform(100, 160);
    sigma2 ~ inv_gamma(1, 1);
    tau    ~ uniform(50, 180);

    // Likelihood:
    for (i in 1:m) {
      // log Q(t_i), computed stably with log_diff_exp
      real logQ = log_diff_exp(normal_lcdf(t[i] | mu, sigma),
                               normal_lcdf(t[i] - tau | mu, sigma));
      target += log(tau) + normal_lpdf(t[i] - y[i] * tau | mu, sigma) - logQ;
    }
  }
"
```

```{r}
#| label: stan-fit
#| echo: false
#| cache: true

library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

# Translate the model to C++ and compile:
stan_mod = stan_model(model_code = modelString)

# Specify data:
stan_data = list(
  m = m, 
  t = day, 
  y = y)

# Generate posterior sample:
stanFit = sampling(stan_mod, 
                    data = stan_data,
                    chains = 3, 
                    iter = 52000, 
                    warmup = 2000, 
                    thin = 1,
                    seed = 2026)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stan
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior summaries for the Type 3 model obtained using Stan (NUTS), based on 3 chains of 50 000 post-warmup draws."
#| echo: false

stan_sum = summary(stanFit, pars = c("mu", "sigma2", "tau", "sigma"),
                   probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))$summary

stan_tab = data.frame(stan_sum[, c("mean", "sd", "2.5%", "50%", "97.5%", "n_eff", "Rhat")])
colnames(stan_tab) = c("Mean", "SD", "2.5%", "Median", "97.5%", "ESS", "$\\hat{R}$")
rownames(stan_tab) = c("$\\mu$", "$\\sigma^2$", "$\\tau$", "$\\sigma$")
stan_tab$ESS = round(stan_tab$ESS)

knitr::kable(stan_tab, digits = 2, escape = FALSE)
```
